tc1.text: Despite the senator’s reputation for blunt speech, her remarks on the treaty were deliberately _____, allowing each faction to hear in them what it wished.
tc1.explanation: “Allowing each faction to hear what it wished” means the remarks could be read several ways; the contrast with blunt speech confirms deliberate vagueness.

tc1.text: The novelist’s early work was lavishly ornate; by contrast, her late prose is almost _____, every unnecessary adjective pared away.
tc1.explanation: “By contrast” with ornate and “pared away” point to plain, severe style; the other choices describe excess.

tc1.text: Critics dismissed the theory as _____, an argument that sounded persuasive on the surface but dissolved under scrutiny; only later did its predictions begin to be confirmed.
tc1.explanation: The colon-like restatement describes something plausible-seeming but unsound, which is specious; cogent would mean the opposite.

tc1.text: Historians once assumed the fashion for powdered wigs was _____, yet it persisted, with minor variations, for nearly a century.
tc1.explanation: “Yet it persisted” signals that the assumption was of brevity, so ephemeral; perennial is the near-opposite trap.

tc1.text: The ministry’s reforms were stymied less by open opposition than by _____ clerks who, without ever refusing an order, simply declined to carry it out.
tc1.explanation: Clerks who quietly resist authority without refusing outright are recalcitrant; the other options suggest cooperation.

tc1.text: Where her colleagues responded to the audit with panic, the director met it with remarkable _____, continuing her routine as though nothing had changed.
tc1.explanation: Calm under pressure in contrast to panic is equanimity; apathy lacks the sense of composure in the face of real concern.

tc1.text: The assassination did not by itself cause the war; it served rather as the _____ that precipitated tensions already long accumulated.
tc1.explanation: “Rather than cause” and “precipitated” describe something that triggers a reaction without being its source; a precursor merely comes earlier.

tc1.text: Because the dam could not eliminate flooding altogether, engineers sought only to _____ its worst effects.
tc1.explanation: “Only” and “could not eliminate” indicate lessening rather than removing; negate would overstate the goal.

tc1.text: Rather than calming the dispute, the mediator’s clumsy remarks served to _____ it, hardening positions on both sides.
tc1.explanation: “Rather than calming” and “hardening” mean the remarks made matters worse.

tc1.text: A judge should be _____ in the case before her, having no financial stake in its outcome, though she should hardly be indifferent to justice itself.
tc1.explanation: Having no stake yet not being indifferent is the distinction that disinterested (impartial) captures; impassive suggests lack of emotion.

tc1.text: The explorer’s journals, unlike the voluble letters he wrote home, are strikingly _____, often recording a week’s march in a single line.
tc1.explanation: A week summed up in one line, contrasted with voluble letters, means terse; meticulous would imply detail.

tc1.text: His lectures were accurate but _____, dwelling on trivial points of terminology at the expense of the argument’s larger sweep.
tc1.explanation: Excessive concern with trivial detail at the cost of the big picture defines pedantic; erudite is a flattering trap.

tc1.text: Though trained in the classical tradition, the young architect became notably _____, delighting in assaults on the conventions her teachers revered.
tc1.explanation: Delighting in attacking revered conventions is iconoclastic; reverent is the opposite.

tc1.text: Reviewers found the debut novel competent but _____; nearly every scene echoed some more inventive predecessor.
tc1.explanation: Echoing predecessors means unoriginal, i.e. derivative; eclectic suggests deliberate variety of sources, not mere echo.

tc1.text: The dish, though hailed as subtle, struck most diners as merely _____, with no distinct flavor to remember.
tc1.explanation: “Merely” and “no distinct flavor” reveal that subtle was an overgenerous label for bland; pungent is the opposite.

tc1.text: Physicians once prescribed a stay in the mountains for the _____ effect of its dry air on the lungs.
tc1.explanation: A medical recommendation implies a health-giving effect; rarefied fits mountain air but not the logic of a prescription.

tc1.text: The courtier’s _____ manner, bowing at every remark of the king’s, made it impossible to know what he truly thought.
tc1.explanation: Excessive bowing that hides true opinion is obsequious; officious means meddlesome, not servile.

tc1.text: Though a brilliant scholar, he was notoriously _____ at dinner, interrupting hosts and ridiculing their opinions.
tc1.explanation: “Though a brilliant scholar” sets up a contrast with rude behavior; interrupting and ridiculing is boorish.

tc1.text: Forgers who escape detection are rarely brilliant artists; they are _____ copyists, indifferent to originality but obsessive about the exact grain of the paper.
tc1.explanation: “Obsessive about the exact grain” defines extreme care for detail, meticulous.

tc1.text: After the deadline passed, the team’s efforts became _____: a few hours of work one day, then nothing for a week.
tc1.explanation: Work that starts and stops without steady purpose is desultory; assiduous is its opposite.

tc1.text: Having won the election by a narrow margin, she showed _____ by appointing several of her fiercest critics to her cabinet.
tc1.explanation: Generosity toward rivals after victory is magnanimity; deference would imply submission to them.

tc1.text: Her _____, reflected in patched coats and unlit rooms, puzzled neighbors who knew she had inherited a fortune.
tc1.explanation: Poverty words are traps; the puzzle is that she chose thrift despite wealth.

tc1.text: The economist has a _____ for contrarian positions, adopting them almost reflexively whenever consensus forms.
tc1.explanation: A reflexive habitual taste for contrarianism is a penchant; antipathy would reverse the sense.

tc1.text: The _____ of surviving manuscripts forces scholars to build elaborate theories upon a handful of fragments.
tc1.explanation: Building theories on a handful of fragments signals scarcity, paucity.

tc1.text: Far from lacking evidence, the investigators faced a _____ of it, and the difficulty lay in deciding which documents mattered.
tc1.explanation: “Far from lacking” and the difficulty of choosing show excess, plethora.

tc1.text: The storm showed no inclination to _____ even after midnight; if anything, the wind grew fiercer.
tc1.explanation: “If anything, the wind grew fiercer” shows the storm did not subside, abate.

tc1.text: Pamphleteers who _____ rebellion rarely anticipate how quickly it will escape their control.
tc1.explanation: Stirring up rebellion that then escapes control is foment; the others imply calming or excusing.

tc1.text: The governor moved quickly to _____ a strike by granting concessions before the union could issue its demands.
tc1.explanation: Acting “before” demands are issued signals preventing in advance, forestall.

tc1.text: The cheerful tone of her letters _____ the hardship she was actually enduring.
tc1.explanation: A cheerful tone set against real hardship means the tone gives a false impression, belie.

tc1.text: The prosecutor could allege fraud but could not _____ the claim with a single verifiable record.
tc1.explanation: “Could allege but could not” points to supporting a claim with proof, substantiate; refute is the trap.

tc1.text: Rather than merely denying the charge, the defense sought to _____ it by presenting records proving the defendant was abroad.
tc1.explanation: Going beyond denial to prove it false is refute.

tc1.text: The witness would _____ his innocence repeatedly, though no one had yet accused him.
tc1.explanation: Repeatedly asserting innocence is averring; gainsay means deny.

tc1.text: Pressed on whether he would raise taxes, the candidate chose to _____, offering a long answer that committed him to nothing.
tc1.explanation: A long non-committal answer is equivocation.

tc1.text: A skilled diplomat must sometimes _____, concealing real intentions behind a mask of affability.
tc1.explanation: Concealing intentions behind a mask is dissembling; disseminate looks similar but means spread.

tc1.text: The printing press allowed reformers to _____ their ideas far more widely than sermons ever could.
tc1.explanation: Spreading ideas widely is disseminate.

tc1.text: The editor’s task was to _____ eight hundred pages of testimony into a coherent forty-page summary.
tc1.explanation: Reducing to an essence is distill; the others add or swell.

tc1.text: Memoirists often _____ the facts, adding colorful detail that improves the story but strains credibility.
tc1.explanation: Adding colorful, strained detail is embellishment.

tc1.text: The treaty’s opening article was meant to _____ the boundary precisely, leaving no room for later dispute.
tc1.explanation: Precise description of a boundary is delineate.

tc1.text: Improved sanitation did not merely treat cholera; it served to _____ the need for treatment by preventing the disease in the first place.
tc1.explanation: Making treatment unnecessary is obviate.

tc1.text: Dense undergrowth did not halt the expedition but did _____ its progress to a crawl.
tc1.explanation: Slowing without stopping is impede.

tc1.text: The new data did little to _____ the hypothesis; if anything, they exposed its weakest assumptions.
tc1.explanation: Data exposing weaknesses do not support the hypothesis, so bolster fits the negated claim.

tc1.text: Rivals sought to _____ her achievements by attributing them to luck rather than ability.
tc1.explanation: Attributing success to luck belittles it, denigrate.

tc1.text: Critics who had ignored his earlier books now _____ him as the finest stylist of his generation.
tc1.explanation: “Now” signals a reversal; praising him as finest is laud.

tc1.text: Skeptics _____ the early aviators as reckless dreamers, until the first successful flights silenced them.
tc1.explanation: Being silenced by success implies they had been mocking, deride.

tc1.text: Followers _____ the founder to such a degree that criticizing him was regarded as sacrilege.
tc1.explanation: Criticism as sacrilege indicates reverence, venerate; emulate means imitate.

tc1.text: Young poets of the period sought to _____ their master, imitating his diction and meter.
tc1.explanation: Imitating diction and meter is emulation.

tc1.text: When relativity came to _____ Newtonian mechanics, the older theory remained the practical tool for ordinary speeds.
tc1.explanation: Replacing a theory in rank while it remains useful is supersede.

tc1.text: Facing public outrage, the board voted to _____ the policy it had adopted only a week earlier.
tc1.explanation: Reversing a policy because of outrage is rescind.

tc1.text: The church declined to _____ the practice, though it never formally forbade it.
tc1.explanation: “Never formally forbade” implies it also did not officially approve; proscribe is the trap.

tc1.text: The council voted to _____ the sale of tobacco near schools, although enforcement remained lax.
tc1.explanation: A ban that is weakly enforced is proscribed; the others suggest permission.

tc1.text: The lecture began as measured analysis but soon degenerated into a _____ against the university administration.
tc1.explanation: Degeneration from measured analysis implies a bitter verbal attack, diatribe.

tc1.text: The professor’s tangent about medieval brewing was an amusing _____, but it left students unsure what had become of the main argument.
tc1.explanation: A tangent away from the main argument is a digression.

tc1.text: The commencement speaker offered one _____ after another, none of which anyone would remember.
tc1.explanation: Unmemorable, stale remarks are platitudes.

tc1.text: ‘Collateral damage’ is a _____ that softens the fact of civilian deaths.
tc1.explanation: A mild phrase substituted for a harsh reality is a euphemism.

tc1.text: Claiming that the novel changed every reader’s life is pardonable _____, but no review should be taken literally.
tc1.explanation: Not to be taken literally signals exaggeration, hyperbole.

tc1.text: The jury faced a genuine _____: acquitting would free a probably guilty man, yet convicting rested on evidence it distrusted.
tc1.explanation: The colon explains a perplexing dilemma, a conundrum.

tc1.text: An unexplained _____ between the ledger and the receipts first aroused the auditor’s suspicion.
tc1.explanation: Two records failing to agree reveals a discrepancy.

tc1.text: A wristwatch glinting on a Roman senator in the film was a jarring _____.
tc1.explanation: Something out of its historical period is an anachronism.

tc1.text: Her essay challenges the neat _____ between reason and emotion, showing that each shapes the other.
tc1.explanation: A sharp two-part division that the essay disputes is a dichotomy; spectrum is the near-opposite.

tc1.text: Opinion on the policy did not split into two camps but ranged across a broad _____.
tc1.explanation: “Not two camps but ranged” implies a continuum, spectrum.

tc1.text: The obituary was less a sober account than a _____, praising its subject without a single qualification.
tc1.explanation: Unqualified praise defines a eulogy.

tc1.text: The final paragraph, a brief _____ restating the opening image, rounded off the essay.
tc1.explanation: A short concluding passage is a coda.

tc1.text: Before stating the actual provisions, the statute offers a lengthy _____ explaining the legislature’s motives.
tc1.explanation: An introductory statement before provisions is a preamble.

tc1.text: Mental illness once carried a _____ so strong that families concealed afflicted relatives.
tc1.explanation: Concealing relatives reflects social disgrace, stigma.

tc1.text: The young composer craved the _____ of critics, yet when it finally came she found it hollow.
tc1.explanation: Craved and finally received suggests approval, approbation.

tc1.text: Executives who defied the boycott met the public’s _____, and several resigned.
tc1.explanation: Resignation after defiance implies public disgrace, opprobrium.

tc1.text: A stickler for _____, the hostess was scandalized when guests removed their shoes.
tc1.explanation: Scandal at breaches of etiquette points to concern for propriety.

tc1.text: He had the _____ to ask for a raise on the very day he was reprimanded for negligence.
tc1.explanation: Brazen boldness in poor circumstances is effrontery.

tc1.text: Voters trusted him not for his charm but for his _____; in thirty years no one had questioned his honesty.
tc1.explanation: Unquestioned honesty is probity.

tc1.text: The merchant’s fortune was built on legal _____: forged contracts and deliberately misleading ledgers.
tc1.explanation: Forged contracts and misleading ledgers signal trickery, chicanery.

tc1.text: After the harvest, the village sank into a seasonal _____, with fields empty and little to do.
tc1.explanation: A lull with nothing to do implies sluggish inactivity, torpor.

tc1.text: Far from showing reluctance, the clerks accepted the extra work with _____.
tc1.explanation: “Far from reluctance” indicates eager readiness, alacrity.

tc1.text: The heat induced a general _____ so thorough that even speaking required effort.
tc1.explanation: Speech requiring effort shows weary listlessness, lassitude.

tc1.text: Nationalist _____ swept the provinces, and calm debate gave way to rallies and marches.
tc1.explanation: Rallies replacing calm debate show passionate intensity, fervor.

tc1.text: In ordinary times the law forbids such searches, but the _____ of the emergency may justify them.
tc1.explanation: “In ordinary times… but” sets up the pressing demands of the emergency, exigency.

tc1.text: Having been swindled once by a plausible stranger, the usually _____ investor grew suspicious of every pitch.
tc1.explanation: The shift to suspicion after being swindled implies he used to believe too easily.

tc1.text: A _____ collector, she could distinguish a genuine Ming vase from a skilled reproduction at a glance.
tc1.explanation: Telling genuine from fake at a glance shows keen judgment.

tc1.text: Her _____ manner disarmed even the cynical; she seemed incapable of calculation.
tc1.explanation: Incapable of calculation means without guile.

tc1.text: The minister’s claim to be surprised by the scandal was _____: memos prove he had known for months.
tc1.explanation: Feigned surprise contradicted by memos is insincere, disingenuous.

tc1.text: The memoir is so _____ that historians cannot cite a single episode without independent confirmation.
tc1.explanation: Needing independent confirmation for everything implies habitual lying.

tc1.text: Though less vivid than other chroniclers, he was the most _____, and historians rely on him whenever accounts differ.
tc1.explanation: “Though less vivid” and reliance on him point to truthfulness.

tc1.text: The lawyer’s closing argument was not eloquent so much as _____: each point followed necessarily from the last.
tc1.explanation: Points following necessarily from one another is convincing logic, cogent.

tc1.text: The plot grew so _____ that readers needed diagrams to track who had betrayed whom.
tc1.explanation: Needing diagrams indicates intricate complication.

tc1.text: Despite the difficulty of the subject, the physicist’s explanation was remarkably _____, and even novices followed it.
tc1.explanation: Novices following a hard subject means clear.

tc1.text: Her dissertation concerns a topic so _____ that perhaps a dozen scholars worldwide could evaluate it.
tc1.explanation: Only a dozen able to evaluate it means understood by few, esoteric.

tc1.text: The film’s dialogue was _____, a string of lines any viewer could have predicted.
tc1.explanation: Predictable lines are unoriginal, banal.

tc1.text: What seemed at first a casual remark proved _____, reorienting the whole field’s assumptions.
tc1.explanation: “Proved” after “seemed casual” and reorienting assumptions means deeply significant.

tc1.text: Though the editor treated the typo as a disaster, the author regarded it as wholly _____, since it altered no meaning.
tc1.explanation: Altering no meaning means unimportant.

tc1.text: The footnotes are not strictly necessary; the material is _____ to the central argument and could be removed.
tc1.explanation: Removable material is only marginally connected, tangential.

tc1.text: Risk is not an accidental feature of investing but an _____ one, built into the very activity.
tc1.explanation: “Built into” means intrinsic, inherent.

tc1.text: The link between the two events is _____, resting on a single coincidence of dates.
tc1.explanation: Resting on one coincidence means weak, tenuous.

tc1.text: Nineteenth-century geologists treated species as _____, though fossils increasingly suggested otherwise.
tc1.explanation: Fossils suggesting change opposes the belief in unchangeable species.

tc1.text: Early childhood is regarded as the period when character is most _____, easily shaped by experience.
tc1.explanation: Easily shaped means malleable.

tc1.text: Neither entreaties nor bribes moved the _____ judge, who had made up his mind before the hearing began.
tc1.explanation: Unmoved by entreaties and bribes means stubborn, obdurate.

tc1.text: Hamlet is often read as an _____ prince, perpetually wavering between vengeance and doubt.
tc1.explanation: Perpetual wavering is irresolution; implacable would mean unrelenting.

tc1.text: The market remained _____, with prices that could swing ten percent within a single afternoon.
tc1.explanation: Wild price swings define volatility.

tc1.text: The volcano had been _____ for centuries, so the residents built farms on its slopes; its sudden eruption startled them.
tc1.explanation: Building farms and being startled indicate a long inactive state.

tc1.text: Her finances were _____: a single missed paycheck would have cost her the apartment.
tc1.explanation: Vulnerable to one missed paycheck means unstable, precarious.

tc1.text: Visitors marveled that the reef, though thousands of tourists came yearly, remained _____, free of any trace of damage.
tc1.explanation: “Free of any trace of damage” means unspoiled, pristine.

tc1.text: Because the data were consistent except for one _____ measurement, the team suspected an instrument fault.
tc1.explanation: One measurement departing from the rest is anomalous.

tc2.text: Although the senator's early speeches were (i) _____, offering little beyond rhetorical flourish, her later budget analyses were so (ii) _____ that even her adversaries conceded the force of her reasoning.
tc2.explanation: “Little beyond rhetorical flourish” signals inflated, empty speech, and “although” sets up a contrast with later analyses persuasive enough to win over opponents.

tc2.text: Colleagues who dismissed the archaeologist as (i) _____ for refusing to publish before her results were replicated overlooked that such caution is the hallmark of a (ii) _____ scientist.
tc2.explanation: The critics’ charge is indecision; the writer corrects it by calling the same caution careful and exacting, the opposite of a casual or whimsical worker.

tc2.text: The economist's model seemed (i) _____ on paper, but it proved (ii) _____ in practice, its tidy assumptions about rational consumers collapsing as soon as real ones behaved otherwise.
tc2.explanation: “Seemed … on paper, but proved … in practice” sets a contrast: workable in theory, shaky in application, as the collapse of assumptions shows.

tc2.text: Far from being (i) _____ about his convictions, the novelist was so (ii) _____ that he interrupted dinner parties to lecture guests on tariff policy.
tc2.explanation: “Far from” negates silence about his views; lecturing at dinner shows he was talkative to excess, not terse.

tc2.text: The first compound is (i) _____ to moisture, so laboratories need no special storage for it; its cousin, by contrast, is so (ii) _____ that one humid afternoon can ruin an entire batch.
tc2.explanation: No special storage is needed only if water cannot get in; the cousin, ruined by humidity, must let moisture through.

tc2.text: Critics dismissed the reformer's program as a mere (i) _____, a lofty sentiment with no mechanism for carrying it out; her defenders conceded the charge but insisted that a (ii) _____ is sometimes needed before details can be settled.
tc2.explanation: A sentiment without mechanism is a platitude, and the defenders’ concession turns on something that comes before details, a preamble, not an ending (coda) or lament (dirge).

tc2.text: The diplomat's manner was so (i) _____ that observers took her for a naif, yet beneath it lay a negotiator so (ii) _____ that she never surrendered a point she valued.
tc2.explanation: “Yet” signals a contrast: an innocent surface over an unyielding core, so the second word must mean stubborn, not yielding.

tc2.text: Far from the (i) _____ manner of her youth, thick with ornament, her late prose is (ii) _____, stripped of everything inessential.
tc2.explanation: The late style contrasts with youthful ornament, so the first blank is showy and the second plain and bare.

tc2.text: Since the treaty's language was deliberately (i) _____, each signatory could claim victory, but that same vagueness would (ii) _____ later disputes by leaving every clause open to rival readings.
tc2.explanation: Vagueness permitting rival readings produces, rather than prevents, disputes; obviate and forestall are the near-opposite traps.

tc2.text: The coach's indiscriminate praise failed to (i) _____ the team's confidence, for approval bestowed on every effort, however (ii) _____, soon lost all meaning.
tc2.explanation: Praise handed out to everything, even half-hearted effort, cannot strengthen confidence; the second blank names the sort of effort that fails to merit praise.

tc2.text: Although the report purported to be a strictly (i) _____ study, grounded in data rather than opinion, its authors, each of whom stood to profit from the merger, were hardly (ii) _____ parties.
tc2.explanation: A claim to rest on data is empirical; the authors’ financial stake undercuts any claim that they were free of self-interest.

tc2.text: Once dismissed as (i) _____, a pale echo of his predecessors, the poet is now hailed as a (ii) _____ of originality.
tc2.explanation: Being an echo means unoriginal, so the early charge is derivative; the reversal makes him a model of originality.

tc2.text: Economists who treat consumers as a (i) _____ mass, each responding identically to price, overlook how (ii) _____ demand can be, swinging with every rumor.
tc2.explanation: Responding identically implies a uniform mass; demand that swings with rumor is changeable, the opposite of the model’s assumed regularity.

tc2.text: The physician cautioned that the symptom, though (i) _____ in most patients, could in rare cases presage something grave and should therefore never be dismissed as (ii) _____.
tc2.explanation: “Though … in most patients” concedes harmlessness, but the warning concerns treating it as unimportant.

tc2.text: The dynasty's (i) _____, a seclusion that kept it ignorant of provincial grievances, made its sudden collapse hardly (ii) _____ ; the unrest had been building for decades.
tc2.explanation: Seclusion is insularity; since unrest had long been building, the collapse was not an aberration.

tc2.text: Rather than (i) _____ the disputants with conciliatory words, the mediator chose to (ii) _____ the quarrel, trusting that open conflict would clear the air.
tc2.explanation: “Rather than” sets up opposites: soothing is rejected and stirring up the quarrel is chosen.

tc2.text: Though the biography is the product of (i) _____ research, every claim footnoted, its author's undisguised (ii) _____ toward the subject colors every judgment.
tc2.explanation: “Though” contrasts thorough research with a bias; only hostility could color every judgment, while apathy or calm would not.

tc2.text: The critic's praise was so (i) _____ that readers suspected flattery; her later (ii) _____ against the same author, equally immoderate, convinced them she simply lacked a sense of proportion.
tc2.explanation: Excess in both directions is the point: groveling praise, then an equally immoderate attack.

tc2.text: Scientists once assumed the Arctic ecosystem was (i) _____, changing only over millennia, but data now reveal it to be (ii) _____, shifting dramatically within a single decade.
tc2.explanation: A system presumed calm and slow-changing contrasts with one that shifts abruptly.

tc2.text: A (i) _____ reading of the contract would confine it to the parties named, but a more (ii) _____ interpretation, attentive to what the signers surely intended, extends its terms to their successors.
tc2.explanation: Confining to the letter is pedantic; looking to purpose is practical.

tc2.text: The old guard was (i) _____, rejecting the new method without ever testing it, whereas the young researchers were (ii) _____, accepting no claim until it had been checked against the data.
tc2.explanation: “Whereas” contrasts untested rejection with careful evaluation; the young group is discriminating, not credulous.

tc2.text: By the third act the play begins to (i) _____, its dialogue repeating itself, and only the lead actor's (ii) _____ keeps the audience from leaving.
tc2.explanation: A play that is weakening needs an energizing counterweight, which is the lead’s passion rather than more listlessness.

tc2.text: The vaccine's (i) _____ was beyond doubt in the trial, since almost none of the treated contracted the disease; yet its maker's claim of universal protection was (ii) _____, ignoring the few who fell ill.
tc2.explanation: Few infections shows effectiveness; “universal” overreaches because exceptions exist, so that claim is flawed.

tc2.text: The sociologist argued that the (i) _____ between “public” and “private” life, long assumed to be sharp, is in fact (ii) _____, the two realms shading into each other.
tc2.explanation: A supposed sharp division is a dichotomy; shading together means the boundary is permeable, not sealed or separate.

tc2.text: Although the CEO appeared (i) _____ when discussing the acquisition's risks, privately she was (ii) _____, scouring reports for any sign of trouble.
tc2.explanation: A calm public face contrasts with private vigilance.

tc2.text: Finding that the defendant had been merely careless and not malicious, the tribunal chose to (i) _____ him of the harsher charge and to (ii) _____ the lesser one, which carelessness plainly supported.
tc2.explanation: Lack of malice clears him of the severe charge, while carelessness confirms the lesser.

tc2.text: The benefits of the mayor's reforms were so (i) _____ that residents could scarcely perceive them, and her insistence on celebrating them struck many as (ii) _____.
tc2.explanation: Barely perceptible benefits are slight; boasting about slight gains is overweening.

tc2.text: The pigment is so (i) _____ that murals painted five centuries ago retain their brilliance, whereas the organic dyes of the same era are (ii) _____, fading within decades.
tc2.explanation: Lasting brilliance implies unchanging pigment; dyes that fade quickly are short-lived.

tc2.text: The historian's (i) _____ for grand narratives led her to (ii) _____ any evidence that complicated them.
tc2.explanation: A fondness for tidy narratives leads to brushing aside inconvenient evidence.

tc2.text: Having lived for decades as a (i) _____, shunning all company, the poet was astonished to find herself, late in life, at the center of a (ii) _____ circle of admirers.
tc2.explanation: Shunning company defines a recluse; the surprise comes from a sociable circle.

tc2.text: Though often called a lament, the memoir is in fact a (i) _____, praising the vanished world rather than a (ii) _____ mourning it.
tc2.explanation: Praise is a eulogy; a lament for the dead is a dirge.

tc2.text: The witness's account was so marked by (i) _____ that, with dates that disagreed and details that contradicted one another, the jury could not (ii) _____ any part of it.
tc2.explanation: Mutually contradictory details are incongruity; the jury cannot confirm any of it.

tc2.text: The engineers refused to let the project's scale (i) _____ them; instead they allowed it to (ii) _____ them to redoubled effort.
tc2.explanation: “Instead” reverses discouragement into spurring.

tc2.text: The senator's gift for compromise was (i) _____ rather than principled: she yielded whenever pressed, then described each retreat as an act of (ii) _____.
tc2.explanation: Yielding under pressure is cowardly, and she dresses retreats up as generosity.

tc2.text: Scholars once regarded the folktale as an (i) _____ text, handed down unchanged, but field recordings show it to be (ii) _____, reshaped by every teller.
tc2.explanation: Handed down unchanged means fixed; reshaped by tellers means pliable, whereas intractable and refractory mean resistant to change.

tc2.text: Neither advocates nor opponents could rally the public, whose (i) _____ was so (ii) _____ that no argument, however stirring, produced a reaction.
tc2.explanation: No reaction at all indicates indifference, deep enough to resist stirring arguments.

tc2.text: The explorer's published account was (i) _____, thick with invented perils, and her own diaries (ii) _____ it, describing an uneventful crossing.
tc2.explanation: Invented perils are lies, and diaries describing calm contradict them.

tc2.text: The glaze was so (i) _____, thick and slow to pour, that potters would (ii) _____ it with water before use.
tc2.explanation: Thickness calls for thinning, not drenching or drying.

tc2.text: To the old guard the young director's insistence on unscripted scenes was heresy; to his admirers it was the mark of an (i) _____ spirit, one that treated every convention as an invitation to (ii) _____.
tc2.explanation: Heresy to traditionalists is iconoclasm to admirers, and treating conventions as invitations means defying them.

tc2.text: The philosopher's argument seems airtight only if one grants its (i) _____ assumption, namely that all rational agents share the same goals; once that assumption is questioned, the whole proof will (ii) _____.
tc2.explanation: An unstated premise on which everything rests; when it is questioned, the structure collapses.

tc2.text: Admirers praised the architect's (i) _____ designs, which drew on sources from many traditions, yet her harshest critics saw only (ii) _____: a refusal to commit to any single vision.
tc2.explanation: Drawing from many traditions is eclectic; critics recast the same trait as an inability to choose.

tc2.text: The medieval chronicler is valued less for his (i) _____ reportage, since he errs often, than for the (ii) _____ of customs he records, many of them noted nowhere else.
tc2.explanation: Frequent errors rule out accuracy as the value; the recompense is abundance of detail, not scarcity or mere confusion.

tc2.text: Because the species is (i) _____ to the island, found nowhere else, its survival hangs by a (ii) _____ thread.
tc2.explanation: Found only on the island means native to it, and with nowhere else to survive its hold is slender.

tc2.text: Although the minister's apology was (i) _____ in form, it was (ii) _____ in substance, expressing regret for the “misunderstanding” without admitting any wrongdoing.
tc2.explanation: A repentant-sounding apology that concedes nothing is insincere.

tc2.text: The statute's structure is (i) _____, with clauses added over decades, each answering a passing crisis, and the result is a (ii) _____ code that few lawyers fully understand.
tc2.explanation: Piecemeal accretion yields incoherence and, from that, an intricate code hard to follow.

tc2.text: Asked about the expedition's chances, the explorer was (i) _____, voicing neither hope nor despair; her sponsors, who wanted a visibly ardent leader, found her (ii) _____ temperament a liability.
tc2.explanation: No visible emotion contrasts with the sponsors’ wish for ardor; the temperament that shows little feeling is phlegmatic.

tc2.text: Her (i) _____ for acquiring rare books left her in (ii) _____, yet she insisted that the library she had amassed was the only wealth worth owning.
tc2.explanation: A habit of buying leads to poverty; “yet” introduces her contrary view of wealth.

tc2.text: Contrary to the view that the policy was a (i) _____ response to crisis, the archives reveal years of planning; far from being (ii) _____, the measure was the logical outcome of long discussion.
tc2.explanation: Years of planning refute hastiness and show the policy was not a departure from the norm.

tc2.text: While the first translation is (i) _____, rendering each word with a dull fidelity, the second is (ii) _____, sacrificing exactness in order to recapture the original's music.
tc2.explanation: Plodding literalism contrasts with an apt, musical rendering.

tc2.text: The theorist's claim that all societies pass through the same stages once seemed (i) _____, but fieldwork would (ii) _____ it, turning up cultures that followed no such pattern.
tc2.explanation: Cultures that follow no pattern disprove it, though the claim once appeared justified.

tc2.text: Though never an aristocrat, the writer found it easy to (i) _____ about his origins, and his (ii) _____ was uncovered only when his tailor's bills surfaced.
tc2.explanation: Concealing origins is dissembling, and the deception is later exposed.

tc2.text: Economists disagree whether the inflation would (i) _____ unaided or was structural; the central bank's (ii) _____ response suggests it believed the former, since it did almost nothing.
tc2.explanation: Doing almost nothing implies the bank expected inflation to fade by itself.

tc2.text: At first the junior partner seemed (i) _____ to every demand, but as the firm's fortunes waned she grew (ii) _____, refusing even routine requests.
tc2.explanation: Initial docility yields to stubborn resistance.

tc2.text: Scholars long regarded the charter as the (i) _____ of later statutes, but new dating shows those statutes predate it; the charter is thus no source but a (ii) _____ of existing law.
tc2.explanation: Revised dating reverses cause and effect: the charter gathers existing law rather than seeding it.

tc2.text: The jurist tended to (i) _____, hedging every opinion, which frustrated clerks who wanted a clear rule; yet the very (ii) _____ of her doctrine let her rulings survive changes in political fashion.
tc2.explanation: Hedging is equivocation; the flexibility that annoys clerks is also what lets the rulings adapt.

tc2.text: He was buried under a (i) _____ of conflicting reports that, rather than clarifying the matter, only served to (ii) _____ the inquiry.
tc2.explanation: A confused mass of reports hinders rather than helps.

tc2.text: The poet affected a lofty (i) _____, but his letters reveal a man racked by (ii) _____ about his own talent, forever soliciting reassurance.
tc2.explanation: Seeking constant reassurance exposes self-doubt behind a pose of calm.

tc2.text: Social scientists distinguish between (i) _____ factors, those woven into a society's structure, and (ii) _____ ones, which arise from chance events and might easily not have occurred.
tc2.explanation: Built-in factors versus occasional, chance ones.

tc2.text: The dean's rhetoric was (i) _____, sounding profound while saying nothing, so students who sought a (ii) _____ answer about tuition left each meeting more confused than when they arrived.
tc2.explanation: Pompous language that obscures leaves students who wanted a clear answer baffled.

tc2.text: Her (i) _____ nature made her a gifted host, but she found the solitude of the research station (ii) _____: after two months without conversation she was desperate for company.
tc2.explanation: A talkative person finds enforced silence burdensome.

tc2.text: The union leader's (i) _____ tone, careful to wound no one, soothed the owners, but the rank and file wanted a fighter and mistook her tact for a (ii) _____ spirit.
tc2.explanation: Soothing tact is conciliatory, and the militants misread it as cowardice.

tc2.text: Though the committee's members agreed on the goal, their methods were so (i) _____ that the final proposal was less a coherent plan than an (ii) _____ of incompatible fragments.
tc2.explanation: Methods that clash yield a mere collection of pieces rather than a unified plan.

tc2.text: The scandal did little to (i) _____ the mayor's popularity; supporters (ii) _____ her lapses as youthful folly and rallied around her.
tc2.explanation: Supporters rallying shows no damage and implies they excused the lapses.

tc2.text: Researchers expected the drug to (i) _____ the illness's symptoms; instead it (ii) _____ them, so that treated patients fared worse than controls.
tc2.explanation: “Fared worse” shows the drug did the opposite of the intended relief.

tc2.text: A good translator must resist the temptation to (i) _____ the source, adding flourishes of her own; the best versions are (ii) _____, content to let the original's strangeness stand.
tc2.explanation: Adding flourishes is embellishing, and the best translations show restraint.

tc2.text: The scientist was a notorious (i) _____, repeating an experiment dozens of times, and she regarded colleagues who accepted a single result as dangerously (ii) _____.
tc2.explanation: Repeated checking marks a skeptic, who sees quick acceptance as credulity.

tc2.text: The first draft of the constitution was (i) _____, covering every contingency in exhaustive detail, whereas the final version is (ii) _____, stating principles and leaving their application to future courts.
tc2.explanation: Exhaustive detail versus terse statement of principles.

tc2.text: The minister had no power to (i) _____ the old treaty on her own, yet she acted as though she did, and parliament, rather than (ii) _____ her, let the announcement stand.
tc2.explanation: Cancelling a treaty alone oversteps; lack of objection means parliament did not rebuke her.

tc2.text: Often dismissed as (i) _____, of interest only to initiates, the philosophy of mathematics has proved (ii) _____, its questions surfacing in every working mathematician's practice.
tc2.explanation: The reputation for obscurity is contradicted by the subject’s presence everywhere.

tc2.text: The CEO would (i) _____ the board's concerns without even reading the memo, a gesture typical of an executive whose (ii) _____ had hardened into contempt.
tc2.explanation: Waving away concerns unread shows brazen disrespect.

tc2.text: Because the drug's side effects are so (i) _____ that doctors rarely hesitate to prescribe it, safety is no obstacle; the real barrier is its price, which is (ii) _____ for many patients who need it.
tc2.explanation: Mild effects are harmless; unaffordable price is the real barrier.

tc2.text: A master of (i) _____, the minister could dress any harsh measure in soothing words; his deputy, by contrast, spoke with such (ii) _____ bluntness that audiences winced.
tc2.explanation: Soothing words for harsh things are euphemism; the contrasting deputy is biting.

tc2.text: The empire's rapid growth, far from strengthening it, hastened its (i) _____, since each conquered province brought rebellion; by the end, the court could not (ii) _____ even the loyalty of its core.
tc2.explanation: Rebellions break an empire up, and a failing court cannot draw out loyalty.

tc2.text: In a state of (i) _____, where every duty is fixed by custom, innovation is rare; in a state of (ii) _____, by contrast, where authority has collapsed, no common rule governs behavior.
tc2.explanation: Custom-bound conformity versus the collapse of authority.

tc2.text: From a handful of similar crimes nearby, the prosecutor drew a sweeping (i) _____ that the defendant must have committed this one, a leap the judge ruled (ii) _____.
tc2.explanation: Projecting from a few cases is extrapolation, and a judge would reject such a leap as superficially plausible but unsound.

tc2.text: Even the most (i) _____ historian, trained to withhold judgment, may find that after years among a figure's letters her (ii) _____ yields to affection.
tc2.explanation: A detached scholar’s calm gives way to feeling.

tc2.text: Her later works do not (i) _____ the visual language of her youth; they (ii) _____ from it so radically that critics speak of two distinct careers.
tc2.explanation: Two distinct careers means not imitating and instead departing.

tc2.text: Reviewers praised the film's (i) _____ photography, whose polished surfaces and burnished light were pure pleasure, but faulted a script so (ii) _____ that each line seemed lifted from a greeting card.
tc2.explanation: Beautiful lighting versus clichéd dialogue.

tc2.text: Skeptics argued that the new theory was so hedged as to be (i) _____, and that a theory which no observation could (ii) _____ was worth nothing.
tc2.explanation: Over-qualification makes a claim unfixable; a theory that cannot be disproved is empty.

tc2.text: The neighbors, who had mistaken the old woman's (i) _____ for (ii) _____, were astonished to learn that her estate, left to the library, was far larger than anyone suspected.
tc2.explanation: Thrifty habits looked like poverty, but her large estate shows she was not poor.

tc3.text: Critics expected the novelist's second book to be (i) _____, a cautious repetition of her debut, yet it proved (ii) _____: it abandoned her earlier conventions so thoroughly that reviewers could scarcely regard it as (iii) _____ to the first.
tc3.explanation: The expectation of repetition suggests derivative, and the 'yet' reverses it to iconoclastic, a book that breaks conventions. A work that abandons its predecessor's conventions could hardly be called analogous to it.

tc3.text: The minister's speech was (i) _____ in tone but (ii) _____ in substance: its soothing language promised relief, yet it offered no measure that could actually (iii) _____ the hardship of the unemployed.
tc3.explanation: Soothing language makes the tone conciliatory, while the contrast with 'yet' shows the substance was perfunctory, offering nothing. Relief that is only promised means no measure could alleviate hardship.

tc3.text: Although early geologists read the strata as evidence of a (i) _____ upheaval, a single catastrophe, later researchers found a (ii) _____ record of slow deposition, so the older view came to seem (iii) _____.
tc3.explanation: A single catastrophe is sudden, hence precipitate. Slow deposition is documented by a careful, meticulous record, and evidence against the catastrophe view makes it specious rather than warranted.

tc3.text: The skeptic's challenge is not that knowledge is impossible but that most of our confident claims are (i) _____: they rest on a (ii) _____ so deeply buried that we never notice it. To (iii) _____ such assumptions is the philosopher's first task.
tc3.explanation: Claims resting on a hidden foundation are tenuous, and that foundation is a supposition. The philosopher's task is to draw such buried assumptions out, that is, to elicit them, not to strengthen or excuse them.

tc3.text: The poet's later work stands apart from the (i) _____ manner of her youthful verse; it is spare and (ii) _____, for she had come to distrust ornament, and where she once would (iii) _____ a line with metaphors she now let plain statement stand.
tc3.explanation: Distrust of ornament marks a break from her earlier grandiloquent manner toward an austere one. Her former practice of adding metaphors to a line is to embellish it.

tc3.text: Researchers cautioned that the correlation, though (i) _____ across datasets, should not be read as causal. Because the survey was voluntary, respondents formed a (ii) _____ group drawn mostly from people with strong opinions, a bias that could (iii) _____ the sample's claim to represent the population.
tc3.explanation: The concession 'though' implies the correlation is robustly present, pervasive. Respondents drawn from one kind of person are homogeneous, which would belie, not support, a claim of representativeness.

tc3.text: Historians once treated the treaty as a (i) _____ event, an abrupt break with the past. More recent scholarship stresses its (ii) _____ character: the clauses merely codified arrangements that had long been (iii) _____ in diplomatic practice.
tc3.explanation: An abrupt break is a discrete event; the revised view says the treaty was derivative of what came before, merely codifying arrangements already implicit in practice.

tc3.text: The painter's reputation rests on an (i) _____: she was at once the most (ii) _____ of colorists, flouting every rule of harmony, and the most disciplined of draftsmen. Critics who admire only one side tend to (iii) _____ the other.
tc3.explanation: Two opposed traits in one artist make an incongruity. Flouting rules is iconoclastic, and partial admirers would disparage whichever side they do not value.

tc3.text: The firm's frugality was (i) _____ to its founder's character, yet years of easy profit would (ii) _____ his successors until they grew (iii) _____ with money, and the company was bankrupt within a decade.
tc3.explanation: Frugality was inherent to the founder; comfortable profits would enervate the successors, who then became prodigal, the opposite of frugal, leading to bankruptcy.

tc3.text: Because the enzyme is (i) _____ at low temperatures, it was long assumed absent from the cells; only when researchers warmed the samples did the (ii) _____ activity prove (iii) _____ after all.
tc3.explanation: Hidden activity that appears only when warmed is latent, since the enzyme is quiescent in the cold. 'After all' reverses the assumption of absence, so the activity proves pervasive.

tc3.text: Although her critics labeled the senator (i) _____, a politician who bent with every poll, her record reveals a (ii) _____ commitment to a handful of causes from which she has never been known to (iii) _____.
tc3.explanation: Bending with polls is irresolute, and 'although' sets up a deep, profound commitment; never departing from causes means never diverging from them.

tc3.text: The committee's report, a bewildering (i) _____ of statistics with little interpretation, left readers to (ii) _____ their own conclusions, a task made (iii) _____ by the report's disorganized structure.
tc3.explanation: Many statistics without interpretation form a welter. Readers must delineate conclusions themselves, and disorganization makes that work arduous.

tc3.text: Far from being (i) _____, as her detractors claim, the memoirist's account is (ii) _____ about its own limits; she repeatedly admits that memory is (iii) _____ and that certain scenes may have been reshaped.
tc3.explanation: Her detractors call her dishonest (mendacious); the rebuttal is that she is ingenuous, openly frank, about the limits of her account, admitting memory is malleable.

tc3.text: A modern speaker who is (i) _____ to the origins of a word would be surprised that it once denoted praise rather than censure; learning this would (ii) _____ him. Such semantic (iii) _____ is common in the history of any vocabulary.
tc3.explanation: A speaker unaware of origins is insensible to them. A reversal of meaning would confound him, and the change itself is a metamorphosis.

tc3.text: Policymakers who treat inflation as a (i) _____ problem, solvable by a single decisive act, ignore how (ii) _____ its causes are; the price of grain, wages, and credit interact so that remedies applied to one often (iii) _____ distress in another.
tc3.explanation: A self-contained problem is discrete; interacting causes are convoluted; and remedies in one area can engender, or create, distress in another.

tc3.text: A hypothesis that can accommodate any outcome is not (i) _____ but (ii) _____: since no observation could (iii) _____ it, it tells us nothing about the world.
tc3.explanation: An unfalsifiable claim is not cogent but specious, seemingly sound yet empty, because nothing could refute it.

tc3.text: The monarch's piety was (i) _____: he prayed publicly and endowed chapels, yet courtiers knew he would (ii) _____ the church's authority whenever it threatened to (iii) _____ his ambitions.
tc3.explanation: Public display marks ostentatious piety, and 'yet' signals that he would flout church authority when it threatened to impede his plans.

tc3.text: Naturalists once presumed the island's birds to be (i) _____, unchanged since arrival; yet comparison of beak sizes across decades shows marked (ii) _____, shifting in response to drought, a pattern that tends to (iii) _____ the older assumption.
tc3.explanation: Unchanged since arrival means immutable. Beaks that shift show plasticity, which belies the older assumption.

tc3.text: The orator was (i) _____: his speeches ran on, filled with (ii) _____ that dazzled the crowd but, on reflection, could not (iii) _____ his claims.
tc3.explanation: Long speeches mark a garrulous speaker. Dazzling exaggeration is hyperbole, and showy language cannot substantiate claims.

tc3.text: Though she professed (i) _____ toward the proposal, her questions revealed a (ii) _____ suspicion; she was not merely (iii) _____ but actively hostile, and the pretense of neutrality deceived no one.
tc3.explanation: Professed neutrality is apathy. Her questions exposed a hidden, latent suspicion, and 'not merely wary but actively hostile' completes the escalation.

tc3.text: The treatise remains (i) _____ to all but specialists: its argument is (ii) _____, dense with technical vocabulary, and its author seems to (iii) _____ any attempt at clarity.
tc3.explanation: A text closed to nonspecialists is recondite. Dense, technical reasoning is convoluted, and an author indifferent to readers would repudiate clarity.

tc3.text: Rather than (i) _____ the dispute, the mediator's remarks only served to (ii) _____ it; a tactful silence would have been more (iii) _____ than her long speech.
tc3.explanation: 'Rather than' sets up the contrast mitigate versus exacerbate. Silence would have been better, more felicitous, than her speech.

tc3.text: The historian's tone is (i) _____: she neither (ii) _____ the explorer nor condemns him, preferring to (iii) _____ the evidence and let readers judge.
tc3.explanation: 'Neither...nor condemns' requires an opposite of condemnation, venerate. A disinterested historian would delineate the evidence rather than embellish it.

tc3.text: Defenders call the tax (i) _____ for its revenue yield, but critics warn that it threatens to (ii) _____ investment so severely that it may ultimately (iii) _____ the very revenue it was meant to collect.
tc3.explanation: Defenders find it viable as a source of revenue; critics say it would impair investment and so attenuate the revenue that rested on it.

tc3.text: The architect's early buildings were (i) _____; every surface was crowded with ornament. Late in life, however, she renounced such excess and produced work of almost (ii) _____ restraint, as if she wished to (iii) _____ her youthful exuberance.
tc3.explanation: Crowded ornament is ostentatious. Renouncing excess yields ascetic restraint, and the late style repudiates the early exuberance.

tc3.text: The parasite's life cycle seems (i) _____: its larvae lie (ii) _____ for months in the soil and then, for reasons not understood, (iii) _____ in a single season.
tc3.explanation: Unexplained abrupt changes make the cycle seem capricious. Larvae lying inactive are dormant, and a sudden surge means they proliferate.

tc3.text: The coalition was held together less by shared principle than by (i) _____: each faction was prepared to (ii) _____ its own program to second place, tolerating the others' only because defeat would (iii) _____ them all.
tc3.explanation: Pressing necessity, exigency, binds them. Each would relegate its program, accepting others' because defeat would discredit all.

tc3.text: To (i) _____ a motive is not to (ii) _____ the act it produced: a judge may recognize the pressures behind a crime and still (iii) _____ the criminal.
tc3.explanation: Describing a motive, delineating it, does not mean condoning the act. A judge may still reproach, not exculpate, the offender.

tc3.text: Sociologists once regarded the village as (i) _____, sealed off from outside influence; yet its (ii) _____ boundaries admitted traders, rumors, and fashions, and the notion of (iii) _____ turns out to be a flattering myth.
tc3.explanation: Sealed off means impermeable. Boundaries that let things in are porous, which undercuts the myth of insularity.

tc3.text: The reviewer's praise is (i) _____: beneath its courtesy lies a bitterness that, by the final paragraph, he can no longer (ii) _____; his last compliment is plainly (iii) _____.
tc3.explanation: Courtesy hiding bitterness is disingenuous. He can no longer dissemble, and the final remark is caustic.

tc3.text: The reformers were (i) _____, convinced that every institution could be perfected; the old magistrate, by contrast, was a confirmed (ii) _____, doubting that any human arrangement would ever (iii) _____ the failings of those who ran it.
tc3.explanation: Confident reformers are ebullient; the magistrate, by contrast, a skeptic, doubts any system could obviate human failings.

tc3.text: Economists note that the market for the rare coin is (i) _____: prices (ii) _____ wildly with every rumor of a new discovery, so that any forecast, however (iii) _____, is likely to be overturned within weeks.
tc3.explanation: Prices swinging with rumor mean a volatile market in which prices oscillate. Even a meticulous forecast would be overturned.

tc3.text: A good experiment isolates a single variable; one that (i) _____ several at once yields results that cannot (ii) _____ any single hypothesis. Such a design is not merely weak but (iii) _____.
tc3.explanation: A design that mixes variables confounds them, so its results cannot substantiate one hypothesis, and the design is fallacious.

tc3.text: The novel's narrator is in truth (i) _____: she claims objectivity yet is careful to (ii) _____ every detail that might reflect poorly on herself, so the reader must (iii) _____ the truth from what she leaves out.
tc3.explanation: A narrator who shields herself is partisan despite claimed objectivity; she occludes unflattering details, and the reader must distill the truth from the gaps.

tc3.text: The explorer's journals, once prized as (i) _____ documents, are now treated as (ii) _____: scholars note that he had every reason to (iii) _____ his hardships in order to secure funding for a second expedition.
tc3.explanation: Once prized as truthful, veracious, the journals are now problematic because the author had motive to embellish his hardships.

tc3.text: Habituation explains why the constant hum of a refrigerator soon becomes (i) _____: repetition makes the brain (ii) _____ to a stimulus that carries no new information, and only a sudden change can (iii) _____ attention.
tc3.explanation: A hum that no longer matters is inconsequential; the brain becomes inured to repetition; a sudden change can elicit attention.

tc3.text: The charity's founder was (i) _____ in giving yet (ii) _____ in manner: he demanded (iii) _____ from every recipient.
tc3.explanation: He gave generously (beneficent) but was meddlingly overbearing (officious), the opposite of obsequious, so he demanded deference.

tc3.text: Early models of the atmosphere treated its layers as (i) _____, each essentially identical throughout; (ii) _____ measurements have since revealed pockets of widely differing temperature within a single layer, a finding that tends to (iii) _____ the older picture.
tc3.explanation: Layers identical throughout are homogeneous. Instrument-based data are empirical, and pockets of difference belie the old picture.

tc3.text: On the strict view, an act done merely to win applause has no moral (i) _____, however (ii) _____ its consequences; a clumsy kindness honestly meant, by contrast, may earn praise that is fully (iii) _____.
tc3.explanation: Acting for applause lacks moral probity however beneficent the results, while an honest gesture earns warranted praise.

tc3.text: Contemporaries were quick to (i) _____ the physicist's early papers as slight, but his insights proved (ii) _____, serving as a (iii) _____ to the field's later development.
tc3.explanation: 'But' reverses dismissing the papers as slight: the insights proved profound and were a precursor to later work.

se.text: Despite decades of mounting evidence and the pleas of his own colleagues, the director proved so _____ on the question of revising the museum's founding charter that every compromise was rebuffed.
se.explanation: Both obdurate and intractable mean stubbornly unyielding, which fits the rebuffing of every compromise; the other choices describe flexibility or caprice.

se.text: Ordinarily voluble in faculty meetings, the physicist grew strikingly _____ when asked about the failed replication, offering a word or two before changing the subject.
se.explanation: Laconic and reticent both mean sparing of speech, matching the contrast with her usual volubility; garrulous and loquacious are the opposite.

se.text: Contrary to the stereotype of the taciturn scholar, the archivist was so _____ that visitors who came for a single document often left an hour later, having heard her entire career.
se.explanation: Garrulous and loquacious both mean talkative, which explains the hour-long visits; laconic and reticent mean the opposite.

se.text: Critics dismissed the novel's closing chapters as so _____ that readers promised a bold resolution received only stock phrases and predictable gestures.
se.explanation: Banal and insipid both mean flat, trite and unstimulating, matching stock phrases and predictable gestures; pungent and caustic imply sharpness.

se.text: The mayor hoped that a modest tax rebate would _____ the angry shopkeepers, who had threatened to shut their stores in protest.
se.explanation: Mollify and placate both mean to soothe anger; the remaining verbs would worsen or stir up the shopkeepers' anger.

se.text: Although the new irrigation scheme could not end the region's drought, engineers claimed it would at least _____ the worst of its effects on subsistence farmers.
se.explanation: Alleviate and mitigate both mean to lessen the severity of something, which fits the concessive 'at least'; the others would worsen or spread the harm.

se.text: Rather than engage with the substance of her theory, her rivals sought to _____ its author, dwelling on her humble origins and lack of credentials.
se.explanation: Denigrate and disparage both mean to belittle, which fits attacking the author instead of the argument; laud and venerate mean the reverse.

se.text: Facing the tribunal, the astronomer was ordered to _____ his claim that the planets orbit the sun, though he privately never abandoned the idea.
se.explanation: Recant and repudiate both mean to formally renounce a claim, which is what the tribunal demanded; aver and the others would affirm or support it.

se.text: Throughout the negotiations the senator seemed to _____ between outright support for the treaty and flat opposition, never settling on a position.
se.explanation: Vacillate and oscillate both mean to swing back and forth, matching the shifts between two positions; the other verbs do not take 'between' this way.

se.text: Pressed by reporters about the budget deficit, the minister continued to _____, offering ambiguous phrases that neither confirmed nor denied the figures.
se.explanation: Equivocate and prevaricate both mean to speak evasively; the other verbs involve plain assertion, proof or praise.

se.text: To _____ their contention that the epidemic began in the harbor district, the researchers compiled shipping records and hospital admissions.
se.explanation: Bolster and buttress both mean to reinforce, which fits the evidence gathered; refute, negate and belie would undermine the contention.

se.text: Following the invention of movable type, small presses began to _____ across the Rhineland, and within a generation hundreds had appeared.
se.explanation: Proliferate and burgeon both mean to multiply or grow rapidly, matching hundreds appearing in a generation; subside and abate mean the reverse.

se.text: The ethics board refused to _____ practices that endangered research subjects, no matter how profitable they proved.
se.explanation: Condone and sanction both mean to approve or permit; the board's refusal makes sense only with these, since proscribing or repudiating risky practices is what it would do.

se.text: Only after the monsoon rains began to _____ did the stranded villagers dare to cross the river.
se.explanation: Abate and subside both mean to lessen, which is why crossing became safe; inundate and saturate would worsen the flooding.

se.text: Economists warned that rigid austerity could _____ the very resentment that populist movements exploit.
se.explanation: Engender and foment both mean to give rise to or stir up; assuage and mollify would calm resentment, and obviate would prevent it, none of which suits a warning.

se.text: Subsequent reforms did much to _____ conditions in the textile mills, though they hardly eliminated hardship.
se.explanation: Ameliorate and enhance both mean to make better, which fits the partial success implied; impair and impede would make conditions worse.

se.text: The headmaster chose to _____ the students gently rather than punish them, hoping that a mild rebuke would suffice.
se.explanation: Reproach and admonish both mean to scold mildly, matching 'a mild rebuke'; laud and venerate mean praise.

se.text: Not even his harshest critics could _____ the evidence, which had been reproduced in three independent laboratories.
se.explanation: Gainsay and refute both mean to deny or disprove, which suits critics who cannot fault reproduced evidence; the others would assert or support it.

se.text: Evening news programs _____ viewers with trivial updates until genuine events lose the power to startle.
se.explanation: Inundate and saturate both mean to overwhelm by excess, which explains why real events no longer startle; the others do not fit the sense of overload.

se.text: The candidate's address, billed as a policy speech, degenerated into a bitter _____ against the press.
se.explanation: Diatribe and tirade both mean a prolonged bitter verbal attack; eulogy and elegy mourn or praise, and preamble and coda are opening and closing parts.

se.text: Though the poet's work now commands high prices, she spent most of her life in _____, relying on friends for rent.
se.explanation: Penury and indigence both mean extreme poverty, contrasting with her later prices; frugality names thrift, not destitution, and the others are unrelated.

se.text: Facing a _____ of contradictory proposals, the committee could not agree on even a procedure for choosing among them.
se.explanation: Plethora and welter both suggest a bewildering abundance; paucity and penury mean scarcity, and a spectrum implies orderly range rather than confusion.

se.text: Months of isolation induced in the crew a profound _____, so that even urgent repairs were left undone.
se.explanation: Lassitude and torpor both mean listless sluggishness, explaining the neglected repairs; fervor and alacrity mean eagerness.

se.text: Even as a child she showed a _____ for dismantling machines to learn how they worked.
se.explanation: Propensity and penchant both mean a natural inclination; antipathy would be dislike, which the curiosity contradicts.

se.text: Among the courtiers, the most _____ was the one who flattered the king constantly while ridiculing him in private.
se.explanation: Obsequious and fawning both mean servilely flattering; perfidious fits the private mockery but means treacherous, not flattering.

se.text: The monastery's _____ regimen, with one meal daily, no heat in winter and silence after dusk, attracted only the most dedicated novices.
se.explanation: Ascetic and austere both mean rigorously self-denying and plain; the others describe showy, lavish or sociable behavior.

se.text: The cartographer was so _____ in checking every coordinate that the atlas took twice as long as planned but contained no errors.
se.explanation: Meticulous and assiduous both convey painstaking diligence, which explains the delay and the lack of errors; perfunctory and desultory mean careless or haphazard.

se.text: The lecture on Etruscan funerary inscriptions was so _____ that even specialists in neighboring fields struggled to follow it.
se.explanation: Esoteric and recondite both mean understood by only a few, which explains the specialists' struggle; lucid and cogent would make it easy to follow.

se.text: Because the single _____ measurement lay far outside the pattern of all the others, the team suspected instrument error rather than a new phenomenon.
se.explanation: Aberrant and anomalous both mean deviating from the norm; analogous and homogeneous suggest similarity, which the outlier lacks.

se.text: Though never written into the bylaws, the _____ understanding among members was that no one would challenge the founder's authority.
se.explanation: Implicit and tacit both mean understood without being stated, matching 'never written'; ambiguous would conflict with a clear shared expectation.

se.text: Unlike the stubborn elder, the younger council members proved _____, willing to reshape their proposals in response to criticism.
se.explanation: Tractable and malleable both mean easily led or shaped, matching their willingness to revise; recalcitrant and refractory mean resistant.

se.text: The new clerk was so _____ that he agreed to every request, however unreasonable, rather than risk displeasing a superior.
se.explanation: Compliant and complaisant both mean eager to go along with others; the remaining choices describe hostile or unyielding temperaments.

se.text: The alliance, held together by a single marriage and a few secret promises, was so _____ by 1450 that a minor dispute could have dissolved it.
se.explanation: Precarious and tenuous both mean flimsy and liable to collapse; immutable and perennial suggest permanence.

se.text: For centuries the volcano remained _____, so villagers built homes on its slopes, unaware that it was merely waiting.
se.explanation: Quiescent and dormant both mean inactive but capable of reawakening; volatile and capricious would signal danger the villagers would have noticed.

se.text: The geologist noted that the clay layer was _____ to water, which explained why the reservoir above it never drained.
se.explanation: Impermeable and impervious both mean allowing no passage of water, explaining the undrained reservoir; permeable and porous are the opposite.

se.text: The assignment proved so _____ that two researchers resigned before the first season's fieldwork was complete.
se.explanation: Onerous and arduous both mean burdensome and demanding, which could drive resignations; the others describe something easy, harmless or clear.

se.text: The emperor's _____ decrees, banning red cloaks one week and requiring them the next, left his courtiers perpetually guessing.
se.explanation: Capricious and whimsical both mean governed by sudden unpredictable impulse; immutable and meticulous suggest constancy or care.

se.text: Jurors described the defendant as strangely _____, showing no flicker of emotion as the verdict was read.
se.explanation: Impassive and stolid both mean showing no emotion, matching the lack of any flicker; the other choices imply visible feeling.

se.text: After the long rainy season, the once energetic crew became so _____ that the schedule slipped by weeks.
se.explanation: Lethargic and indolent both mean sluggish and disinclined to work, explaining the delay; assiduous and ebullient are the opposite.

se.text: The general's _____ speeches, stuffed with inflated phrases about destiny, embarrassed even his allies.
se.explanation: Bombastic and grandiloquent both mean pompously inflated in language; laconic and reticent mean sparing of words.

se.text: Corruption was no occasional lapse; it was _____ throughout the regime, found in every ministry.
se.explanation: Pervasive and endemic both mean widespread and ingrained; sporadic and ephemeral would mean occasional or fleeting, contradicting 'every ministry'.

se.text: The argument, though superficially plausible, was ultimately _____, resting on an equivocation between two senses of 'free'.
se.explanation: Fallacious and specious both mean seemingly sound but actually flawed; cogent and warranted would credit the argument with strength it lacks.

se.text: The _____ young envoy, who assumed that everyone spoke as candidly as he did, was easily outmaneuvered.
se.explanation: Guileless and ingenuous both mean innocently candid, explaining his vulnerability; disingenuous and mendacious imply deceit.

se.text: The editor's _____ examination of the manuscript, a few pages sampled at random and the rest skimmed, let dozens of errors through.
se.explanation: Desultory and perfunctory both describe an unmethodical, cursory effort, matching the random sampling; meticulous and assiduous are the opposite.

se.text: The legal argument followed so _____ a path through precedent that the jurors lost the thread.
se.explanation: Convoluted and tortuous both mean twisting and hard to follow, which explains the lost thread; lucid and cogent would make it easy.

se.text: The reviewer's _____ wit scalded every author unlucky enough to fall under her gaze.
se.explanation: Caustic and pungent both mean sharp and biting, matching 'scalded'; insipid and banal mean bland.

se.text: The composer's final work, a solemn _____ for the victims of the flood, was performed without applause.
se.explanation: Dirge and elegy both mean a mournful composition for the dead, fitting a solemn work for victims; a coda and a preamble are structural parts of a piece.

se.text: To _____ the angry river god, the villagers cast garlands and silver coins into the current each spring.
se.explanation: Appease and propitiate both mean to win over an angered power with offerings; goad and exacerbate would provoke it further.

se.text: Certain ores are _____, resisting the standard smelting methods and forcing metallurgists to devise new ones.
se.explanation: Recalcitrant and refractory both mean resistant to treatment; tractable and malleable mean yielding.

se.text: The _____ intern, who rearranged the director's calendar without being asked, was soon the subject of corridor complaints.
se.explanation: Officious and presumptuous both describe overstepping one's role; reverent, contrite and reticent describe humble or restrained conduct.

se.text: The mosaic's inscription is so worn that its date remains _____, and scholars place it anywhere between the third and sixth century.
se.explanation: Indeterminate and ambiguous both mean not clearly fixed, matching the wide range of proposed dates; lucid would mean clear.

se.text: The author's _____ prose circles each idea for pages before landing on it, taxing even sympathetic readers.
se.explanation: Diffuse and verbose both mean wordy and unfocused, matching the circling; laconic and reticent mean brief.

se.text: The new theory seeks to _____ earlier findings from chemistry and physics into a single framework.
se.explanation: Amalgamate and incorporate both mean to combine into a whole; distill would mean to extract an essence, and the others do not fit 'into a single framework'.

se.text: Her friends' efforts to _____ the widow's grief, though well meant, came to nothing.
se.explanation: Assuage and alleviate both mean to ease; exacerbate and foment would worsen grief, which contradicts 'well meant'.

se.text: Asked whether the audit had found irregularities, the treasurer chose to _____, claiming not to recall the relevant files.
se.explanation: Dissemble and prevaricate both mean to evade the truth, matching the feigned lapse of memory; aver and substantiate involve straightforward assertion.

se.text: Hoping to _____ his reputation before the election, the senator endowed a children's hospital.
se.explanation: Burnish and enhance both mean to improve the luster of something; denigrate and discredit would harm it.

se.text: The general's _____ against deserters lasted twenty minutes and left the assembled recruits silent.
se.explanation: Harangue and invective both mean a forceful verbal attack, matching the silence it produced; eulogy and elegy honor or mourn rather than attack.

se.text: The family endured public _____ for years after the scandal, though none of them had been implicated.
se.explanation: Opprobrium and stigma both mean public disgrace; probity and piety are virtues that would not be endured as a burden.

se.text: Auditors noted a glaring _____ between the two ledgers, though neither clerk could explain it.
se.explanation: Discrepancy and incongruity both mean a lack of agreement between things that should match; the other nouns make no sense with 'between the two ledgers'.

se.text: The court demanded strict _____ from all who entered, forbidding talking, hats and eating.
se.explanation: Decorum and propriety both mean correct, dignified conduct; levity and effrontery are the kind of behavior the rules forbid.

se.text: Despite repeated setbacks, the surveyor's _____ to complete the map never wavered.
se.explanation: Resolve and resolution both mean firm determination, matching 'never wavered'; ambivalence and diffidence suggest doubt.

se.text: Her _____ replies, free of any calculation to please or impress, charmed the interviewers.
se.explanation: Artless and guileless both mean natural and without craft; disingenuous, perfidious and mendacious imply deception.

se.text: The limestone is so _____ that rainwater seeps through it into vast underground caverns.
se.explanation: Permeable and porous both mean allowing liquids to pass through; impermeable and impervious are the opposite.

se.text: Though wealthy, the philosopher led an _____ life, dining on bread and water and refusing all luxuries.
se.explanation: Abstemious and ascetic both mean self-denying, fitting bread and water; prodigal and ostentatious suggest indulgence.

se.text: A civic _____ settled over the district, and fewer than one voter in five bothered to cast a ballot.
se.explanation: Apathy and torpor both mean listless indifference, explaining the low turnout; fervor and alacrity would raise it.

se.text: The minister's decision drew widespread _____ from editorial writers across the political spectrum.
se.explanation: Castigation and opprobrium both mean harsh public criticism; approbation and eulogy mean approval or praise.

se.text: Chronic noise exposure can _____ a child's ability to learn to read.
se.explanation: Impair and impede both mean to hinder; enhance, facilitate and bolster would help.

se.text: Historians must _____ their claims with primary sources rather than rely on family legend.
se.explanation: Substantiate and document both mean to support with evidence; refute and belie would undermine claims.

se.text: Colleagues admired the dispatcher's _____ temperament; while others panicked as the lines lit up, he calmly handled call after call.
se.explanation: Imperturbable and phlegmatic both mean calm and not easily excited; irascible and volatile are the opposite.

se.text: Producers continued to _____ the market with cheap goods until buyers could absorb no more.
se.explanation: Saturate and satiate both mean to fill beyond capacity, matching 'could absorb no more'; stint would mean to supply sparingly.

se.text: Her talent for mathematics lay _____ through childhood, surfacing only when a teacher assigned her a proof.
se.explanation: Latent and dormant both mean present but inactive until awakened; the others do not fit something that surfaced late.

se.text: The two traditions remained _____, sharing no vocabulary, texts or practices until the nineteenth century.
se.explanation: Disparate and discrete both mean separate and distinct; analogous and homogeneous suggest similarity.

se.text: Her reply to the review was so _____, studded with insults and personal abuse, that the journal refused to print it.
se.explanation: Vituperative and caustic both mean harshly abusive, which explains the refusal to print; the others describe respect or flattery.

se.text: The senator's _____ opposition to the bill, which no concession or argument could soften, doomed the compromise.
se.explanation: Obdurate and implacable both mean unyieldingly opposed, matching the failure of every concession; tractable and conciliatory mean yielding.

se.text: The patient was so _____ in refusing every therapy that the clinic eventually closed his file.
se.explanation: Intractable and recalcitrant both mean stubbornly resistant to direction, explaining the closed file; compliant and complaisant mean cooperative.

se.text: The coach tried to _____ the fuming star by offering him a larger role, but he resigned anyway.
se.explanation: Placate and appease both mean to calm by concession, which is what a larger role is for; goad and exacerbate would inflame him.

se.text: Dense forest can _____ the force of a storm surge, absorbing much of its energy before it reaches the town.
